Sample text:
---
### The Lost Property Office

On the morning the city decided to close its lost property office, a man came in looking for a plum.

“Not a particular plum,” he explained. “Any plum would do.”

Nora, who had worked behind the counter for twenty-three years, told him they didn’t keep fruit. It was the sort of thing she usually said without looking up, but that morning she wanted to see who would come all the way down to the basement of the municipal building for a plum.

He was wearing a suit with one sleeve damp to the elbow.

“Did you lose one?” she asked.

“No. My sister used to bring me one when she picked me up from swimming. I’ve just been swimming, and I thought I’d see if I could get the rest of the afternoon right.”

“There’s a grocer on Bell Street,” Nora said.

“I know. I own it.”

He thanked her and left. For the next hour she thought about the damp sleeve.

At eleven, a woman from the city brought down several rolls of colored stickers. Green for auction, red for disposal, yellow for anything that might contain personal data. She stuck a green dot on a violin case without opening it.

“Wouldn’t you want to see if there’s a violin inside?” Nora asked.

“Is there?”

“No.”

The woman peeled off the dot. “Then you’ve saved somebody a disappointment.”

Nora waited until she was gone before opening the case. Inside were three sheets of music and a pencil worn down to the length of a thumbnail. Years ago, a boy had come in with his father to claim it. The father had described a blue case with brass clasps, which was accurate. But when Nora brought it out, the boy took one look and said, “Mine never had a handle.”

The father swore softly. The boy’s face did something Nora had not understood until much later: he was trying not to smile. For a few more hours, at least, he wasn’t going to have to practice.

She put the pencil in her pocket.

Her own daughter had lost a shoe at the seaside when she was six. Nora had made them walk the length of the beach twice looking for it. The girl had found a crab shell, a plastic dinosaur, and a piece of glass worn soft as soap. She had offered each in turn as a reason to stop.

At last Nora had carried her back to the car. She no longer remembered the shoe. She remembered the sandy foot bumping against her thigh.

At lunch she called her daughter and asked if she remembered the shoe.

“What shoe?”

“Never mind. What are you doing?”

“Eating an egg over the sink.”

“Is there something wrong with your table?”

“No, Mum. I just didn’t want to get a plate.”

Nora could hear a tap running. Her daughter asked how the packing was going, and Nora said she was making progress, which was true in the sense that the morning was gone.

By three, she had filled five boxes. By four, she was down to the umbrella stand. The office had once had a policy of keeping umbrellas for ninety days. Then the city reduced it to thirty, and then to seven. There were always about forty umbrellas. People lost them on the first clear afternoon after rain.

Nora took the stand upstairs and set it outside the front doors with a sign that said PLEASE TAKE ONE. On her way back down, she passed the grocer.

He was sitting on the basement steps. He had changed his jacket.

“I thought I’d try again,” he said.

“We still don’t have any plums.”

“I brought some.”

He showed her the paper bag. There were at least a dozen inside, greenish yellow, with small brown freckles. She had expected purple ones.

“Are these the right kind?” Nora asked.

“I haven’t tried one yet.”

She sat beside him, and he chose two. Hers was cold and so ripe that the skin broke under her thumb. She bent over her knees to keep the juice off her blouse. Beside her the grocer laughed, though he hadn’t taken a bite.

“She had a towel,” he said. “That’s what I forgot. She always brought a towel from home because I never dried myself properly. She’d make me stand behind the car and do my ears.”

“How old were you?”

“Thirty-seven.”

Nora looked at him.

“I was learning,” he said. “I’d been afraid of the water.”

He finished his plum, folded the pit into a corner of the bag, and went upstairs. He left the rest of the fruit with Nora. Through the stairwell window she watched him take an umbrella, open it to check the spokes, and put it back. It was a clear afternoon.

At five, the woman from the city returned with a caretaker. He rattled the handle after locking the office, then stooped to peer through the little window in the door.

“You’ve left the light on,” he said.

“I know.”

He waited. Nora had no explanation for him. After a moment he unlocked the door and turned it off himself.

Outside, somebody had taken the entire umbrella stand. Nora caught the bus to her daughter’s apartment with the plums on her lap. At each stop they rolled to one side of the bag, then settled back.

Her daughter answered barefoot, with a dish towel over her shoulder.

“You could have called,” she said.

“I did call.”

“You asked me about a shoe.”

Nora held out the bag. Her daughter looked inside, picked a plum, and went to eat it over the sink. Nora followed. From the kitchen window they could see a man in the building opposite trying to coax a cat in from a ledge. He was shaking a box of something the cat plainly did not want.

Without turning away from the window, Nora’s daughter took the towel off her shoulder and handed it to her. Nora wiped her chin. They stayed there long enough to see the man give up and the cat come in on its own.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet, carefully shaped short story whose recurring objects carry its emotional movement.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and gently wry, finding feeling in small practical details rather than naming it outright: a damp sleeve, a pencil worn to a thumbnail, a sandy foot, plums eaten over the sink. Nora’s grief is understated; closing the office brings old memories into contact with her present distance from her daughter, and the stranger’s story about learning to swim lets Nora recognize something without needing to explain it. The ending offers a modest invitation to notice care when it arrives indirectly: a towel passed over without turning away, and a cat that comes in on its own.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost property, memory, and the objects through which care persists: the violin case, shoe, umbrellas, plums, and towel. It favors tenderness without tidy resolution—the office closes, the shoe remains forgotten, and the daughter does not become suddenly confessional—while allowing small acts of attention to matter.

## Evidence line
> At each stop they rolled to one side of the bag, then settled back.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story is coherent and distinctive, with recurring objects and restrained emotional turns that make its chosen attention to ordinary acts of care unusually revealing.
